items.title: Pretium Statement Regarding Agreement with the Federal Trade Commission
items.description: Pretium Statement Regarding Agreement with the Federal Trade Commission November 6, 2026 --> Pretium and Progress Residential have reached an agreement with the FTC and four states to resolve the Commission’s Civil Investigative Demand related to certain aspects of our resident experience during the period of 2021 to 2025. The agreement contains no admission of wrongdoing, and we maintain that Progress’ practices have been transparent, fair, and consistent with industry practice. Although we disagree with the FTC’s claims, this resolution allows us to move forward with our continued improvements to the experience of our residents and the deployment of capital to expand the availability of quality, affordable rental housing for working families. We welcome the FTC’s efforts to establish uniform, industry-wide standards for the single-family rental industry related to fee disclosures and transparency. Pretium and Progress have led the way in adopting these standards.

items.title: Newly Pending Listings Fell 17% In October, The Biggest Year Over Year Drop Since 2023 (Zillow October Market Report)
items.description: Newly Pending Listings Fell 17% In October, The Biggest Year Over Year Drop Since 2023 (Zillow October Market Report) Completed existing home sales fell 9% annually, according to Zillow’s preliminary sales nowcast. Written by Mischa Fisher on November 5, 2026 Key findings: Zillow’s preliminary measure of existing home sales fell 8.7% year over year in October. Newly pending listings — a leading indicator of next month’s closed sales — fell 16.8% year over year, the biggest decrease since August 2023. The typical mortgage payment in October was 12.8% higher than a year ago, according to Zillow’s estimates. The Zillow Observed Rent Index rose 2.9% year over year in October as the rental market continues to strengthen. The acute sting of suddenly higher mortgage rates is having the unfortunate effect on the housing market that last month’s pending sales data foretold. As mortgage rates entrenched themselves above 7%, home sales slowed sharply in October. Existing home sales fell 8.7% year over year, though that largely reflects sales agreed to in September, when mortgage rates were below 7% for much of the month. Newly pending listings, a leading indicator for the next month’s closed sales, fell 16.8% from last October, marking the biggest annual dip since August 2023 and slowest October since 2018. November is shaping up to have an even larger contraction in sales activity, but the silver lining is that next month is likely going to be the worst of it. The pace of the slowdown is expected to ease into the new year. A jump in housing costs likely drove the slowdown. The monthly mortgage payment on the typical U.S. home was an estimated $2,004 in October, assuming a 20% down payment and excluding taxes and insurance. That’s up 12.8% from last year and 4.8% higher than in September, the biggest one-month jump in four years. For a buyer putting only 5% down and securing an FHA loan, which comes with a lower mortgage rate, the year-over-year rise has been similar at 11.8%. Once insurance, taxes and maintenance are factored in, a median-income household would spend 41.5% of its income on that monthly payment, up from 39.2% a year ago. The rise in mortgage costs is almost exclusively due to higher mortgage rates. The typical U.S. home value fell 0.6% month over month and is just 0.7% higher than a year earlier, as measured by the Zillow Home Value Index. Meanwhile, mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, according to Freddie Mac , up from 6.86% in September. As for-sale activity wanes, the rental market continues to strengthen. The typical U.S. rent is up 2.9% year over year, according to the Zillow Observed Rent Index. That’s the strongest annual gain in the past 19 months, and marks the seventh consecutive month that annual rent growth has increased. While there is no avoiding that this has been a very soft fall for for-sale activity, there are deals to be had for buyers able to brave the affordability headwinds in the coming months. Buyers usually have leverage this time of year when sellers try to make a deal before the holidays, and especially so this year given current market conditions. The continued inventory buildup means there is a lot of upside for sales into next year if we get rate relief. More data, including dashboards with local market data , can be found on the refreshed Zillow Research website . The Zillow November Market Report is expected to be released December 4 . Home Values & Mortgage Payments The typical U.S. home value is $364,812, according to the Zillow Home Value Index (ZHVI). ZHVI fell 0.6% month over month in October. Home values are 0.7% higher than a year earlier. The monthly mortgage payment on a typical U.S. home is $2,004, assuming a 20% down payment and excluding taxes and insurance. That is 12.8% higher than last year. Inventory There were 1.4 million homes for sale nationwide in October. Active inventory was 3.4% higher than a year earlier. Inventory rose 0.4% from September. New for-sale listings totaled 328,328 in October, down 4.2% from a year earlier and down 4.4% from September. Sales 304,105 homes were sold in October, according to the preliminary Zillow sales count nowcast. That is 8.7% lower than a year earlier and down 5.4% from September. These figures will be revised mid-month. Newly pending listings, which measures listings that changed from for-sale to pending status rather than closed sales, shows a 16.8% decrease from a year earlier and a 9.1% decrease over September. Affordability A household earning the median income would need to spend 34.7% of its income on the typical monthly mortgage payment (assuming a typically valued home and a 20% down payment, and including estimates for taxes, maintenance and insurance). That is up from 32.7% a year earlier and up from 33.5% in September. A household earning the median income would need to spend 26% of its income on the typical rent in October. That is unchanged from a year earlier and from September. Competition Homes took a median of 31 days to go pending in October. That was two days longer than a year earlier and two days longer than September. The share of listings with a price cut in October was 26.5%. That was down from 26.9% a year earlier and down from 27.3% in September. 25.6% of homes sold above list price in September, the most recent data available. That’s compared to 25.2% a year earlier and 27.5% in August. Rents The typical rent nationwide is $1,913, according to the Zillow Observed Rent Index. That’s 2.9% higher than a year earlier and flat from September. 40.4% of rental listings on Zillow offered a concession in October. That’s up from 38.7% a year earlier and up from 39.6% in September. While the unemployment rate ticked up from3.9% to 4.4% during that timeframe—and exceeded the national average of 4.2%—the increase was largely attributed to expanded labor force participation, rather than job losses. A key driver of this trend has been the Metro’s strong wage growth, with the median household income rising by 4.6% year-over-year (YOY) to $98,500. Phoenix’s population also grew at four times the rate of the national average, however, the 0.8% YOY increase marked a slowdown from previous quarters. Annual GDP growth, meanwhile, accelerated up from 2.4% in Q3 2025 to 2.7% in Q3 2026, underscoring the Metro’s positive economic momentum. Supply & Demand: Vacancy Plummets Amid Record Demand Net absorption across the Phoenix Metro reached 18,071 units year-to-date (YTD) through Q3 2026, already eclipsing the record annual total of 17,303 units set in 2024. This robust level of absorption, paired with a meaningful slowdown in new deliveries, enabled vacancy to decrease by 200 basis points (bps) YOY to a three-year low of 10.8%. All 15 multifamily submarkets recorded positive absorption for a third consecutive quarter, with Downtown (760 units), Deer Valley (752 units) and South West Valley (665 units) leading the overall market in Q3. Developers completed a six-year low of 2,008 units in Q3 2026. The slowdown in deliveries is likely to continue, with the active pipeline declining to 16,013 units, the lowest level since year-end 2019. During Q3, nine out of 15 submarkets observed no new openings, while just one—East Valley—accounted for 42% (835 units) of the Metro’s total. The East Valley is also the most active submarket for ongoing construction, with 3,838 units, or 24% of the market-wide pipeline. Pricing: Landlords Adjust Asking Rents To Aid Occupancy Rent trends from Q3 2026 suggested that landlords are generally continuing to temper marketed rates to unlock greater levels of renter demand, with the average level decreasing by 0.9% YOY to $1,590 per unit. This dynamic has been widespread, with 10 out of 15 multifamily submarkets posting YOY declines, ranging from 0.5% in the East Valley to 4.3% in Pinal County. Submarkets that observed YOY increases through Q3 include North Scottsdale (1.9%), Chandler (0.9%), Camelback (0.8%), Gilbert (0.4%) and Old Town Scottsdale (0.2%). items.title: Alliance's Industrial Strength Draws Huge Spec Development From Trammell Crow And PGIM
items.description: A joint venture of two commercial real estate powerhouses just broke ground on a massive speculative project in one of Dallas-Fort Worth’s hottest industrial submarkets. Courtesy of Trammell Crow Co. A rendering of the next phase of the Eagle 35 logistics hub in Fort Worth Trammell Crow Co . and joint venture partner PGIM , the investment management arm of Prudential Financial , started work on a nearly 756K SF industrial park in the AllianceTexas area of Fort Worth. The three-building development is the fourth phase of the joint venture’s 35 Eagle logistics hub . ”Dallas-Fort Worth is one of the nation’s most resilient industrial markets, supported by strong demand for modern logistics facilities,” PGIM Real Estate Head of U.S. Equity Soultana Reigle said in a statement. “We see significant opportunity in partnering with TCC to advance this development, meet the evolving needs of today’s industrial users and capitalize on the region’s long-term growth fundamentals.” DFW's industrial leasing total of 22.7M SF during the third quarter nearly matched the region's record total of 23M SF set in Q2 2021, according to the latest data from Cushman & Wakefield . The Alliance area was by far the most popular industrial destination in North Texas, absorbing more than 3.6M SF during the quarter. During the first nine months of the year, Alliance absorbed more than 7.6M SF, double the total of the next-closest submarket in DFW. Alliance’s year-to-date totals of more than 10M SF of leasing activity and 5M SF of deliveries are all also tops in the region. The industrial project from Trammell Crow and PGIM will also add to the submarket’s DFW-leading 8.3M SF under construction. The new phase of 35 Eagle will feature a 508K SF cross-dock building with a 40-foot clear height and up to approximately 450 trailer positions, a 107K SF rear-load building with a 32-foot clear height, and a 140K SF rear-load building with a 32-foot clear height. The buildings are being built on 58 acres at the northwest corner of Interstate 35 West and Eagle Parkway. Fifth Third Bank and American National Bank provided construction financing for the project. Alliance Architects is the project’s architect, FCL Builders is the general contractor, and Halff is the civil engineer. CBRE ’s Steve Trese, Bob Scully, Ahnie Sheehy and Reid Kennedy are handling marketing and leasing for the project. items.title: Annual rent growth sees a milestone, even as prices ease in October
items.description: Annual rent growth sees a milestone, even as prices ease in October by Kim O'Brien Posted November 6, 2026 in Market Research October marked the first month of rent cuts in the U.S. apartment market in 2026, but annual gains continue at a robust pace. Same-store effective asking rents increased 1.7% year-over-year, according to October data from RealPage Market Analytics . That was the market’s biggest annual price increase since May 2023. While the annual reading has improved, the gain stemmed less from robust monthly pricing and more from weak rent performance falling out of the annual calculation. In fact, rents came down a mild 0.7% during October, marking the first monthly rent cut in the U.S. in calendar 2026. U.S. apartment occupancy faded to 95% in October, easing 20 basis points (bps) from the September showing. Still, October occupancy is up 40 bps in the calendar year and remains 10 bps ahead of the October 2025 showing. Helping support occupancy and rent performance, the U.S. apartment market has seen supply and demand edge closer to balance recently. Renters absorbed nearly 304,800 conventional apartments in the year-ending 3rd quarter 2026, gaining ground on a cooling supply wave. Developers completed nearly 318,000 units in the past year, nearly half the recent peak from late 2024. Bay Area and Midwest markets still lead for rent growth Rent performance remained sharply split by market. Coastal tech hubs and Midwest metros delivered the strongest annual gains, while most Sun Belt markets kept logging rent declines. Northern California's tech-driven markets posted the three strongest gains among the 50 largest apartment markets in the year-ending October. San Francisco saw rents hike 14.7% over the past year, San Jose followed at 9.5%, and Oakland reached 8.5%. All three markets are running near 97% occupancy. Midwest markets make up much of the rest of the top 10 list. Milwaukee led the major Midwest markets with annual rent growth of 4.2%, followed by Chicago (3.3%), Kansas City (3.1%) and Cleveland (3.1%). Detroit and St. Louis both fell just shy of making the cut, with annual rent growth of 2.7% in each market. Sun Belt rents still trail, but the gap is narrowing The South region overall has returned to annual rent growth, though barely, at 0.5% in October. Sun Belt and Florida markets continue to see the nation’s steepest declines. San Antonio had the deepest cut among big markets at 2.6%, stemming from occupancy at 92.5%, also dead last among the largest 50 markets. Also posting rent declines in the year-ending October were Houston (-1.8%), Tampa (-1%), Charlotte (-0.9%) and Denver (-0.8%). The bigger story, however, is how many Sun Belt markets have stopped seeing rent positioning hemorrhage. Annual increases have returned to Phoenix (0.4%) and Austin (0.6%), as well as Atlanta (0.8%), Raleigh (1.0%), Miami (0.6%) and Jacksonville (2.6%). items.title: US home price insights — November 2026
items.description: Overview: Home prices continue to rise nationally, up 1.7%, but momentum is moderating with a 0.3% monthly decline, and annual growth forecasted to slow to 0.9%. Compared with August, appreciation strengthened in about half of metros and weakened in the other half, suggesting no single national trajectory. Annual appreciation was led by northeastern and Great Lakes states, paced by Illinois (6.9%), Rhode Island (6.4%), Connecticut (6.0%), New Jersey (5.1%), and Ohio (4.9%). National home price growth September 2026 data Source: Cotality ‍ Affordability meter Source: Cotality ‍ ‍ Market activity will favor regions with solid economic prospects, regions that attract retiring population and offer affordable homes. Dr. Selma Hepp Cotality Chief Economist Insights from Chief Economist Dr. Selma Hepp As autumn arrived, the U.S. housing market cooled further. In September 2026, single-family home prices rose just 1.7% year-over-year and dropped 0.3% from August, pushing the national median above $400,000. This was the largest monthly decline since 2022 and the third consecutive September without growth, as high mortgage rates curbed summer demand. Normally, home prices edge up about 0.2% in September. But national averages still hide a key divide: Every Northeast and Midwest state saw annual price gains, while four Western and two Southern states posted declines. The market is nearly evenly split between areas accelerating and those slowing. Many Northeastern and Midwestern markets have gained 25% to 30% since mid-2022, while much of the West and Texas have seen little or no net growth. This regional divide sharpened considerably heading into the final stretch of the year. Chronic inventory shortages in the Great Lakes and New England fueled strong annual gains— Illinois (6.9%), Rhode Island (6.4%), Connecticut (6.0%), New Jersey (5.1%), and Ohio (4.9%). Meanwhile, prices dropped in former boom states: Washington (-1.0%), Wyoming (-0.7%), Texas (-0.4%), Hawaii (-0.1%), and Utah (-0.0%). Since June 2022, Rhode Island, Connecticut, and New Jersey have surged 30–31%, while Washington, Colorado, and Texas are up less than 1%, and D.C. is down 2%. “Potential homebuyers are feeling the pinch from rising costs across the board, especially for daily living expenses,” said Cotality Chief Economist Dr. Selma Hepp. “Meanwhile, limited job opportunities and slow wage growth are making households reluctant to move.” Leading metros for recent price growth include Cleveland, Albany, Providence, Greensboro, and St. Louis—places marked by affordability, job growth, in-migration, and recent price resets. In contrast, the fastest-cooling markets, like Augusta, Austin, Seattle, San Jose, and Washington, DC, have seen job losses, higher inventory, and declining affordability. Rising mortgage rates have sharply reduced affordability. When the 30-year fixed rate rose from 6.5% to 7.5%, the monthly payment on a median-priced home jumped $300, pushing the required annual income to $103,000. In California, buyers need $180,900 for a $754,500 median home. In Florida and Texas ($369,750 median), higher insurance and taxes often push total costs above borrowing limits, fueling declines in metros like Austin (-2.0%) and Dallas (-1.0%). “Elevated mortgage rates are expected to limit home buying opportunities in 2027,” concluded Dr. Hepp. “However, more inventory and greater buyer bargaining power will keep home price growth subdued, improving affordability. Market activity will favor regions with solid economic prospects, regions that attract retiring population and offer affordable homes.” -Dr. Selma Hepp Cotality’s Chief Economist Dive deeper Home price indexes Top 10 hottest markets Source: Cotality ‍ Top 10 coolest markets Source: Cotality ‍ Which areas are affordable? items.title: Gateway Markets Regain Development Momentum
items.description: Gateway Markets Regain Development Momentum by Chuck Ehmann Posted October 29, 2026 in Multifamily Construction Permits Whether you call them “gateway” markets or the “sexy six,” the primary coastal hubs that traditionally attract the majority of domestic and international capital are well represented among the top markets for annual multifamily permitting in September’s data release from the U.S. Census Bureau, and in most cases are dramatically increasing their permitting activity. New York continues to lead the nation for multifamily permitting with 37,691 units permitted in the year-ending September, an increase of more than 13,000 units from last year or a jump of 52.7%. Los Angeles again ranked #2 with about 18,000 units permitted, almost doubling their annual total from one year ago. Washington, DC remained among the top permitting markets at #5 in September, increasing their annual permitting by 47.4% or about 3,900 units, while Seattle slipped to #11 this month but still increased their multifamily permitting total by 36.7% or roughly 2,400 units. Rounding out the “sexy six,” Boston ranked #16 among Realpage’s top 150 markets with a 44.7% annual increase (+2,303 units) to 7,460 units, while the Bay Area markets of San Jose, Oakland and San Francisco ranked well down the list individually but would have ranked #7 with a combined total of 11,543 units permitted, up 46.8% from last year (+5,407 units). Conversely, among the secondary high-growth markets, development activity has stalled or fallen back as top 10 markets Phoenix and Atlanta permitted close to the same amount as last year, while Dallas, Houston, Austin and Miami decreased their permitted unit counts by a combined 11,004 units. Only Raleigh/Durham saw a significant increase in multifamily permitting (+3,153 units) among the non-gateway top 10 markets. Despite declining permitting in four of September’s top 10 markets, their combined total of 148,456 units was up 14.5% from last September for an increase of 18,765 units. Compared to August, the top 10 markets’ annual permitting total was little changed (-0.7%). In addition to the expanding top 10 and the gateway markets mentioned, other markets with significant increases in annual units permitted in September were Kansas City (+2,187 units), West Palm Beach (+1,932 units), College Station-Bryan, TX (+1,762 units), Tacoma (+1,712 units) and Fort Worth (+1,672 units). Orlando (-4,572 units) led for annual permitting decreases, followed by Dallas and Houston. Significant decreases occurred in Columbus, OH (-2,911 units), Riverside-San Bernardino (-2,162 units), San Diego (-2,100 units) and Lakeland-Winter Haven, FL (-1,995 units). Permitting by Place Below the metro level, eight of August’s top 10 permit-issuing places returned to this month’s list with the first five remaining in order. The list of top individual permitting places (cities, towns, boroughs, and unincorporated counties) generally includes the principal city of some of the most active metro areas. The city of Los Angeles again led the nation for multifamily permitting at the local level with New York’s three most active boroughs returning among the top five. The city of Phoenix also placed in the top five while the city of Fort Worth jumped to #6 in September from #10 last month. The cities of Austin and Atlanta each slipped one spot as the cities of Columbus and Houston fell out of the top 10 entirely. The cities of Miami and Denver joined the top 10 list this month, permitting about 5,500 units apiece. Among the top 10 metros for multifamily permitting, Dallas, Houston, Washington, DC and Raleigh/Durham were not represented on the top 10 list of permitting places, although the core cities of Dallas, Houston, Raleigh and Durham were among the top 20 places. items.title: Q3 multifamily sales jumped 139% on Vivmark deal
items.description: Q3 multifamily sales jumped 139% on Vivmark deal Although the mega-merger made 2026’s third quarter the highest on record, apartment values fell 4.6% year over year and 6.2% at an annualized rate between Q2 and Q3. Published Nov. 2, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google The Avalon at Palisades in Charlotte, North Carolina. AvalonBay Communities acquired the property before it became Vivmark. Permission granted by AvalonBay Communities Dive Brief: The third-quarter apartment sales landscape was very similar to August’s, with sluggish single-asset sales. Still, the merger of Equity Residential and AvalonBay Communities drove deal volume up 139% year over year to $114.1 billion, according to a report that data firm MSCI Real Assets shared with Multifamily Dive. The RCA CPPI for apartments declined 4.6% YOY. It fell 6.2% at an annualized rate between Q2 and Q3, as pricing deteriorated over the past four months. The annualized decline in values in each quarter has outpaced the yearly drop. In contrast, the RCA US National All-Property CPP rose 0.9% YOY. Without the creation of Vivmark, sales would have fallen 7% YOY for the quarter and been flat so far for the first nine months of the year. However, with the deal, 2026’s third quarter was the largest on record, surpassing $90.4 billion in 2021 and $78.4 billion in 2022. It was the second-largest quarter on record, falling only behind Q4 2021, which tallied $167.1 billion in trades. Dive Insight: Prices usually follow transaction growth, with investors underwriting appreciation as they bid, according to MSCI. “Here, volume is rising while prices fall, which points to a single transaction rather than broader confidence in the apartment sector,” MSCI said in the report. The usual gauge of industry health, individual sales, dropped 12% YOY to $34.3 billion in Q3, marking the second straight quarter of decline. In the six major metros, individual sales were approximately flat at $11.8 billion, while they dropped 17% YOY to $22.5 billion in non-major cities. The Vivmark deal pushed up volume across various subtypes. Portfolio sales rose 19% YOY to $10.2 billion on the strength of the Vivmark deal, while mid- and high-rise transactions jumped 248% YOY to $70.2 billion. The market was hardly thriving before the 10-year Treasury began rising six months ago. But since then volumes have declined, and cap rates have risen. In Q1 2022, cap rates sat at 4.5%, according to MSCI’s hedonic rate calculation. Now they’re 140 basis points higher. While much of that movement came in early 2024, they climbed 20 bps over the last year to 5.9% in Q3. As the 10-year Treasury moved above 5% in Q3, owners say it has become difficult to project deals they’re underwriting . “The last 60 days have been difficult, and from our end makes it difficult to pin down where we think exit caps are going,” American South Capital Partners Executive Vice President Tyler Epps told Multifamily Dive. Tyler Chesser, the co-founder and managing partner of CF Capital, said that “cap rates have moved out since the September [Federal Reserve] meeting,” and sellers are slow to accept it. “Historically it takes a few quarters for seller expectations to catch up to the market,” Chesser previously told Multifamily Dive. “Until they do, the bid-ask gap means a lot of deals stall, get retraded, or die.” Click here to sign up to receive multifamily and apartment news like this article in your inbox every weekday. items.title: October 2026 Jobs Report: Employment growth tops market forecasts
items.description: October 2026 Jobs Report: Employment growth tops market forecasts Written by Kenny Lee on November 6, 2026 Key findings U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, while gains in September and August were revised up by a combined 84,000. The unemployment rate slipped to 4.1% from 4.2% as strong employment growth absorbed an increase in labor force participation. Wage growth continued to cool compared to recent years, with average hourly earnings rising 3.1% year over year. What happened: The nonfarm payroll employment rose 165,000 in October, topping financial market expectations. Combined with strong upward revisions to increases in September and August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics report this month indicates a meaningful improvement in job growth. The increases in employment were broad-based across key industries such as professional and business services (+70,000); healthcare and social assistance (+55,000); and transportation and warehousing (+25,000). Employment in temporary help services, a leading indicator for overall labor demand, soared to 18,600. The household survey also indicates a resilient labor market. The labor force participation rate increased to 61.9% from 61.8% as more workers rejoined the workforce. Combined with strong increases in employment, the unemployment rate fell to 4.1% from 4.2%. Why it matters for housing: Stable employment and wage growth give households the confidence to buy a home or sign a new lease, but the housing market is already feeling the chilling effects of the recent surge in mortgage rates. Zillow data points to a colder-than-usual fall market: our preliminary measure of existing home sales fell 8.7% year over year in October. Newly pending listings — a leading indicator of next month’s closed sales — fell 16.8% year over year, the biggest decrease since August 2023. With mortgage rates above 7%, affordability headwinds in the housing market may still feel insurmountable — even for those who have a job or recently found one. This is consistent with our expectation for a more substantial decline in existing home sales and slower growth in home value in Q4. While mortgage rates have been declining from their recent peak, it is difficult to know how far they will fall when forces pushing up Treasury yields, such as anxiety over government deficits and geopolitical impact on energy prices, remain at play. But when mortgage rates come down, eventually, buyers will be ready. The Bureau of Labor Statistics report today is consistent with a stable labor market in a growing economy. The resilient labor market will pave the way for a housing market thaw. items.title: Multifamily Developer Confidence Weakens in Third Quarter
items.description: Multifamily Developer Confidence Weakens in Third Quarter November 5, 2026 Eric Lynch No Comments New multifamily housing confidence weakened year-over-year in the third quarter, according to the Multifamily Market Survey (MMS) by the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB). The MMS produces two separate indices. The Multifamily Production Index (MPI) had a reading of 41, down five points year-over-year, while the Multifamily Occupancy Index (MOI) had a reading of 69, also down five points year-over-year. Developer sentiment for new multifamily production has softened, due to challenges such as high interest rates , construction costs that are high relative to rents, and problems getting projects approved and connected to roads and utilities, resulting in many projects taking longer to complete. Due to the headwinds facing the industry, NAHB’s 2027 forecast shows a decline for multifamily starts. Although the administration’s regulatory reform efforts are helping to ease some cost pressures, the multifamily sector would still benefit from an expedited permit process and lower rates on development and construction loans . Multifamily Production Index (MPI) The MMS asks multifamily developers to rate the current conditions as “good ”, “fair”, or “poor” for multifamily starts in markets where they are active. The index and all its components are scaled so that a number above 50 indicates that more respondents report conditions as good rather than poor. The MPI is a weighted average of four key market segments: three in the built-for-rent market (garden/low-rise, mid/high-rise, and subsidized) and the built-for-sale (or condominium) market. All four components experienced decreases year-over-year and are in negative territory (i.e., below 50) during the third quarter. The component measuring subsidized units fell six points to 49, the component measuring garden/low-rise dropped five points to 48, and both the component measuring mid/high-rise units and the component measuring built-for-sale units decreased four points to 33 and 31, respectively. Multifamily Occupancy Index (MOI) The survey also asks multifamily property owners to rate the current conditions for occupancy of existing rental apartments in markets where they are active as “good”, “fair”, or “poor”. Like the MPI, the MOI and all its components are scaled so that a number above 50 indicates more respondents report that occupancy is good than poor. The MOI is a weighted average of three built-for-rent market segments (garden/low-rise, mid/high-rise, and subsidized). Two of the three components experienced declines year-over-year for the third quarter of 2026. The mid/high-rise component declined seven points to 59 and the garden/low-rise component fell six points to 70. The component measuring subsidized units saw an increase of two points to 83. Nevertheless, all three components remained above the break-even point of 50. Changes in Overall Market Conditions The MMS was re-designed in 2023 to produce results that are easier to interpret and consistent with the proven format of other NAHB industry sentiment surveys. Until there is enough data to seasonally adjust the series, changes in the MMS indices should only be evaluated on a year-over-year basis. For more recent information about the market, the survey contains a separate question asking multifamily developers to compare current market conditions to conditions three months earlier. In the third quarter of 2026, 6% of respondents said the current market is better, and 28% said it is worse. However, the majority of developers—66%—said that the market is currently about the same as it was three months ago. Please visit NAHB’s MMS web page for the full report. items.title: Mortgage Rates Drift Lower, but Spring Shopping Season Might Still See Rates Above 7%
items.description: Mortgage Rates Drift Lower, but Spring Shopping Season Might Still See Rates Above 7% Zillow expects mortgage rates to remain above 7% for the rest of 2026 through mid-2027, presenting a possible headwind for next year’s home shopping season. Written by Kara Ng on November 4, 2026 In short: Mortgage rates are easing from their recent peak, but Zillow expects them to stay above 7% through mid-2027 — likely leading to a chillier 2027 spring home shopping season. Mortgage rates continue to retreat Mortgage rates continue their decline from the recent peak, though they remain challenging for housing affordability. As of November 4, oil prices fell on hopes of easing geopolitical tensions and markets are weighing the potential effects of restrictions on data center construction. Whether the forces keeping bond yields elevated — government deficits, geopolitical impacts on prices, and corporate borrowing to fund AI spending — could sustainably fade remains an open question. Zillow expects mortgage rates to remain above 7% for the rest of 2026 through mid-2027, presenting a possible headwind for next year’s home shopping season. What’s the impact on housing? Challenging affordability continues to weigh on the for-sale market. Newly pending sales, a leading indicator of future closings, fell 17% in October , the biggest year over year drop since 2023. At the same time, rental demand skyrocketed, with rental engagement per listing (as measured by ZORDI ) growing 22% in October compared to last year, as elevated borrowing costs push would-be buyers to rent instead. With little relief in the mortgage rate outlook, the spring 2027 home shopping season could arrive with rates still above 7%, which may hamper activity. items.title: ULI Emerging Trends Report: DFW Three-Peats as Top Market to Watch in 2027, Houston Holds Serve
items.description: ULI Emerging Trends Report: DFW Three-Peats as Top Market to Watch in 2027, Houston Holds Serve by Taylor Williams November 6, 2026 November 6, 2026 4 LAS VEGAS — For the third consecutive year, Dallas-Fort Worth (DFW) has secured the top spot as the U.S. market with the best overall real estate prospects. That’s according to the Emerging Trends in Real Estate 2027 report, which is jointly produced every year by the Urban Land Institute (ULI) and accounting firm PwC. After finishing third and fifth in the 2025 and 2026 rankings, respectively, Houston has more or less maintained the status quo, claiming the No. 6 ranking in the 2027 report. Austin, meanwhile, continued to slip in the rankings, ostensibly due to the market’s ongoing struggles to catch up to recent building booms in the industrial and multifamily sectors. The state capital’s real estate prospects ranked 21st on this year’s list, marking the third consecutive year in which the market has failed to crack the Top 10. In explaining the top ranking, ULI and PwC immediately pointed to t he Texas Stock Exchange (TXSE) , which launched in downtown Dallas earlier this year and has been credited with fueling the growth of a major new vertical within the local economy: financial services. The report identified two nameless financial institutions — known within the real estate community to be Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley — that are developing new office campuses in Uptown Dallas in conjunction with the debut of TXSE. According to the report, combined, these projects could bring as many as 8,800 new jobs to Dallas over the next decade. In addition, the report noted that DFW is a top market for new development of data centers, though a statewide moratorium on permitting of those facilities and questions about the state’s ability to meet power requirements represent concerns to actualizing some of those projects. Oversupply in the metroplex’s industrial market is also burning off thanks to strong absorption of large-format facilities, while absorption of office space is also on the rise in conjunction with residential conversion projects that are putting dents in the existing inventory of vacant office space. Lastly, the report cited the decisions of both the NBA’s Dallas Mavericks and NHL’s Dallas Stars to pursue new arenas and surrounding mixed-use districts as fresh sources of growth on the retail, restaurant and entertainment sectors. The PMMS results are based on data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA): mortgage rates collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . How is the national average determined? We collect the mortgage rate of all purchase applications based on PMMS criteria and a national average mortgage rate is calculated out of all the selected loan applications. PMMS rates are based on applications submitted to Freddie Mac for the given week from lenders across the country. What type of lenders are included in the PMMS? Currently, our lenders are a mix of credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies. Do the PMMS results represent the rates charged on a specific day of the week? If so, which day? Or are they the average rate charged that week? PMMS is published each Thursday at noon ET. When a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, the PMMS will publish on the Wednesday of that week. The week of application activity starts at 12:00 a.m. ET the prior Thursday and lasts through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. Therefore, the PMMS results are an average of loan rates offered Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Why are adjustable rates no longer published? ARMs indexed to alternatives to U.S. Treasury securities have become more prevalent in the market. As we worked on enhancing the PMMS , we carefully considered which loan products were most popular for the PMMS borrower profile (good/excellent credit, 20% loans, home purchase loans on owner occupied 1-unit single-family properties). Additionally, in recent years the mortgage market has been dominated by fixed mortgage products. While there has been an uptick recently in the share of adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for the broader mortgage market, ARMs remain most popular for higher loan size (nonconforming) loans. Why are fees/points no longer published? Under the current LPA requirements, fees and points are not always required to be provided by lenders. Therefore, we are not able to report on the average fees and points. How has PMMS changed over time? Since April 1971, Freddie Mac shared the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate with the PMMS. We have updated the information we collect and the process for gathering data over time. Changes in Data Processes When it was launched, PMMS surveyed lenders on the rates and points for their most popular 30-year fixed-rate, 15-year fixed-rate and 5/1 hybrid amortizing adjustable-rate mortgage products. The survey was based on first-lien prime conventional conforming home purchase mortgages with a loan-to-value of 80 percent. In addition, the adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) products were indexed to U.S. Treasury yields, and lenders were asked for both the initial coupon rate and points as well as the margin on the ARM products. Lenders surveyed each week were a mix of lender types — credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies — roughly proportional to the level of mortgage business that each type commands nationwide. On November 17, 2022, the mortgage rate gathering process was updated. Instead of surveying lenders, we now use data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA). Changes in Information Shared In 1984 , the 1-year ARM was added to the survey. In 1991 , the 15-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was added. In January 2005 , a 5/1 hybrid ARM series was added. items.title: Mortgage Rates Climb in October Amid Accelerating Inflation
items.description: Mortgage Rates Climb in October Amid Accelerating Inflation November 3, 2026 Catherine Koh No Comments Mortgage rates rose sharply again in October as the U.S. treasury yields surged. According to Freddie Mac , the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.33% in October, up 47 basis points (bps) from September. The rate reached 7.40% in early October, its highest level since 2023, before easing toward the end of the month. Since the conflict in the Middle East began, the 30-year mortgage rate has increased by approximately 128 bps. The 15-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.66% in October, up 46 bps from September and 123 bps from the end of February. Compared with a year ago, the average 30-year and 15-year mortgage rates were higher by 108 bps and 117 bps, respectively. The 10-year Treasury yield, a key benchmark for long-term borrowing, increased 21 bps to an average of 5.15% in October, although yields eased during the latter part of the month. Inflation concerns continued to put upward pressure on Treasury yields, as elevated energy prices stemming from the ongoing conflict with Iran contributed to accelerating inflation. Inflation accelerated to 3.7% in September from 3.4% in August. Energy prices were a major contributor, with fuel oil prices rising 15.3% and gasoline prices increasing 9.1% over the month. At its latest meeting, the Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4.00%. However, there were two dissenters who voted for a 25 bps increase. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) described economic activity as expanding at a “strong pace,” an improvement from the “solid pace” noted in September. The committee pointed to resilient consumer spending and strong business investment as signs of continued economic strength, while noting that inflation remained elevated and uncertainty persisted. items.description: October 2026 Monthly Housing Trends: Buyers and Sellers Hit Pause as Rates Surge By Jake Krimmel Nov 04, 2026 Market outlook If September’s slowdown hinted at a fall stall for the housing market, October confirmed it. Mortgage rates peaked at 7.40% in mid-October, capping a six-week 74 basis point surge. And although rates have since eased to 7.24%, the damage to purchasing power has been done. The same monthly principal and interest payment now supports a loan nearly 6% smaller than it did in late August. The October Realtor.com® data show a market where almost everyone has pressed pause for now. Buyers on the sidelines are staying there, and sellers – whether they’re on or off market – are disengaging as well. New listings fell at their fastest rate in three years, while current sellers are not slashing prices or pulling listings at meaningfully higher rates than last year, when falling mortgage rates kept the market unseasonably warm. What happens next depends on the broader economy. A dip in the 10-year Treasury yield could restore some purchasing power, but it could also tempt buyers to wait for further progress. Our base case is that mortgage rates remain above 7% in the near term, with the market facing an early chill as winter approaches. In This Report Top storylines and key questions Core metrics: October 2026 Summary tables Data appendix October’s top storylines, according to the data Buyers pull back, as they battle mortgage rates and loss of purchasing power Pending sales are down 10.5% year over year, the steepest annual decline since October 2023, and contract signings are also down 17%. With 30-year rates averaging 7.33% in October, 107 basis points above a year ago, buyers have lost real purchasing power. Sellers freeze rather than panic New listings fell 7.5% year over year, the steepest drop since September 2023, but delistings and price cuts are moving sideways. About 4.4% of active listings were delisted, versus 4.6% a year ago, and the share with a price cut (20.5%) is just 0.2 points above last year and down from September. Sellers are disengaging rather than showing signs of real distress. About 43% of current active listings have ever had their price reduced, down from nearly 55% a year ago. Inventory growth accelerates for fourth straight month, closest to pre-pandemic norm yet Active listings grew 7.4% year over year, topping 1.18 million homes for sale, the fourth straight month of faster growth. National inventory sits 6.7% below pre-pandemic norms, the narrowest gap we have seen yet. Key questions Q: Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, the highest since 2023. Where is that showing up in the market, and is the impact the same everywhere? A: Even with rates dipping slightly in the latest reading (7.24% on Oct 29, down from 7.40% in mid-October), 30-year rates are still 107 basis points above this time last year and 53 above the start of September. That loss of purchasing power (a 10.4% loss compared to a year ago and a 5.2% loss since the start of September) is showing up first in the demand indicators. The stock of homes under contract is down about 10.5% year over year, contract signings are down by 17%, and mortgage applications for purchase are down more than 18% from a year ago over the past two weeks. Q: Last month, we said sellers were the thing to watch. Are they responding to weaker demand by cutting prices, pulling listings, or sitting out altogether? A: Right now it looks more like a seller pause than an exodus. For the fourth consecutive month, more than 1 in 5 listings saw a price cut, but the share is only 0.2 points above last year and slipped from September. New listings are down year over year at a time of year when they are already seasonally low. Sellers know this is a poor time to list, and you do not list into weak demand unless you need to. What we have not seen is a meaningful increase in delistings. That matters for two reasons. First, sellers are not giving up yet. And second, we also need to reframe the delisting conversation this time of year, because a higher count, even if it were happening, would not signal seller stress as we approach the holidays. A seller throwing in the towel in July is different from one calling it quits around Halloween or nearing Thanksgiving. Q: What should we be monitoring heading into the holiday months as 2026 comes to a close? A: Prices vs. inventory. More inventory and slower sales mean rising months of supply, but if sellers are not cutting prices more deeply, the market may not be getting as buyer-friendly as the inventory numbers imply. List prices are down 2.2%, the 12th straight year-over-year decline, but with mortgage rates still significantly higher than this time last year, potential buyers are still operating at a loss when it comes to purchasing power. The Realtor.com ® 2026Q3 Market Clock® Report found the US housing market is on the cusp of buyer’s market territory, and about two-thirds of the 100 largest metros were either outright buyer’s markets or trending in that direction. Still, buyers gaining ground at the negotiating table is different from gaining enough purchasing power to pull would-be buyers off the sidelines. Until the affordability math shifts notably, do not expect swings in housing demand. items.title: Single-Family Development Remains Constrained
items.description: Single-Family Development Remains Constrained by Chuck Ehmann Posted October 21, 2026 in Multifamily Construction Permits Don't expect single-family construction to accelerate anytime soon. Consumer and builder confidence has weakened, while mortgage rates, financing costs, construction expenses, labor costs and regulatory hurdles continue to weigh on development activity. At the same time, ongoing affordability concerns and elevated home prices are limiting housing demand. Single-family housing starts surged above 1.3 million units on a seasonally adjusted basis during the post-pandemic period of exceptionally low mortgage rates. As borrowing costs climbed and mortgage rates moved above 7%, housing starts fell to roughly 800,000 units by late 2022. Annualized starts activity later recovered to more than one million units before gradually easing back toward 900,000 units in 2026. With mortgage rates averaging roughly 7.4% in October, pressure on the single-family sector is likely to persist. September’s seasonally adjusted rate for single-family starts was 859,000 units, down 4.6% from August’s revised rate but up 2.6% from one year ago. Annualized single-family permits fell 4% from August and 4.8% from last September to a 3.5-year low of 845,000 units. The number of single-family homes currently under construction was unchanged month-to-month at 587,000 units, but that annualized rate was down 2.8% from last September. Single-family completions dipped 2.4% for the month but fell 11% from one year ago to 840,000 units, while units authorized, but not started jumped 6.3% from last year to 151,000 units, the same rate as last month. Meanwhile, multifamily development faces similar headwinds with the seasonally adjusted starts rate at 349,000 units, down 7.2% from August and 25.9% from last year. Annualized multifamily permitting increased 5.9% for the month and 1% for the year to 503,000 units. Reflecting the volatility of the seasonally adjusted data series, the unadjusted annual starts and permits totals for multifamily were both up close to 7% from last September. Like the single-family series, the annualized rate of multifamily units under construction was unchanged for the month at 677,000 units, however, that was down 3.1% for the year. Authorized multifamily units that were not started were also unchanged for the month at 123,000 units but were up 13.9% for the year. Multifamily completions rose 14.9% from August to 339,000 units but were down 20.4% for the year. Compared to one year ago, the annual rate for multifamily permitting increased in two of the four regions, with moderate improvement in the Northeast (up 8.5% to 83,000 units) and solid growth in the Midwest (up 32.8% to 79,000 units). The West region saw the deepest decrease of 17% in annual multifamily permitting to 100,000 units in September, followed by a very modest 0.2% decrease in the South to 241,000 units. Compared to the previous month, permitting was down in the West and up in the remaining regions. Annualized multifamily starts decreased sharply in three regions: the West (down 56.7% to 48,000 units), the Midwest (down 54.4% to 35,000 units) and the Northeast (down 43.5% to 62,000 units). The South region’s multifamily starts increased 16.8% to 205,000 units. Compared to August’s seasonally adjusted annual rate, starts were up strongly in the South and down in the remaining regions. items.title: Mortgage Applications Decline as Higher Rates Boost ARM Share
items.description: Mortgage Applications Decline as Higher Rates Boost ARM Share November 4, 2026 Catherine Koh No Comments Mortgage application activity declined in October as the 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose sharply again . The Mortgage Bankers Association’s (MBA) Market Composite Index, a measure of total mortgage application volume, fell 14.1% month-over-month in October on a seasonally adjusted basis. Compared to a year ago, total mortgage applications were 39.8% lower. Higher fixed mortgage rates continued to drive borrowers toward adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs), whose share of total applications increased to 10.8%. Steep declines occurred in both major components as the average contract rate for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage jumped 35 basis points (bps) to an average of 7.4% in October. Purchase applications decreased 11.9% from September, while refinance applications declined 17.3%. Relative to October 2025, purchase and refinance activity were also down 17.3% and 58.5%, respectively. Meanwhile, the average contract interest rate for 5/1 ARMs was 6.4% in October. The lower initial interest rate and monthly payments made ARMs relatively more attractive to borrowers, contributing to a 0.7% increase month-over-month. Nonetheless, ARMs remained 31.1% lower than a year ago. The ARMs share of total applications for October increased 1.5 percentage points to 10.8%. Meanwhile, applications for fixed-rate mortgages declined 15.5% month-over-month and 40.7% year-over-year. Average loan sizes declined across most categories in October. The overall loan size decreased 1.5% to $375,200. Purchase loans, however, saw a marginal increase of 0.5% to an average loan size of $448,500. Meanwhile, the average refinance loan size declined 8.0% to $257,840, and ARMs loan size declined 4.8% to an average of $854,180. items.title: Mortgage Rates Drop From September Highs as Midterms and Jobs Data Loom
items.description: Mortgage Rates Drop From September Highs as Midterms and Jobs Data Loom Published on November 2nd, 2026 by Chen Zhao In A Nutshell: Rates have fallen about 30–40 basis points since the peak at the end of September and there’s little reason to believe the volatility will slow down. Last Week’s Highlights The Fed meeting last Wednesday was the highlight of the week, with the committee voting to hold rates steady as expected. There were two dissents, with one coming from a surprising source, Governor Lisa Cook, who is usually seen as someone who favors lower rates. The statement and press conference reiterated a desire to keep hiking, making a December hike more likely than not if the economic data comes in as expected. The Fed has been highlighting elevated inflation and strong economic growth as its reason for hiking. And Q3 GDP, in fact, came in at a brisk 3.4% annual rate. Real business fixed investment spending grew at a 12.7% annual rate thanks to rapid growth in AI spending. And real consumption grew at a 3.8% annual rate as people spent out of savings and wealth increases rather than income growth. The question now is what happens to growth in Q4. Real-time data is pointing to a potential slowdown as consumers pull back. Upcoming Attractions It’s another big week with both the midterm election tomorrow and employment data arriving throughout the week. Democrats are expected to comfortably gain a majority in the House of Representatives with control of the Senate also favoring Democrats, but less certain. Expectations for government spending, which has been a factor for rates, could certainly change with a more divided government. But the near term economic impact might be felt most acutely as we near government funding and debt limit deadlines. The closest budget deadline is December 11, which might get pushed to Q1. And we’re likely to hit the debt limit again in Q1 at which point the Treasury will take “extraordinary measures” until we truly run out of options sometime before October 2027. Since it’s the first week of the month, we’ll also get the typical employment reports, including job openings and turnover on Tuesday and the official jobs report on Friday. With the Fed squarely focused on inflation, the jobs report mostly serves as a check on whether the Fed needs to turn its attention back to recession risk, which would reduce the need for the rate hikes that markets have priced in. So far this year, the answer has been “no,” with the labor market on solid enough footing and that is not expected to change with this week’s data. Finally, Fed officials are out of their blackout period following last week’s FOMC meeting. With Chairman Warsh typically reluctant to offer much forward guidance, markets have been relying more on surrogates to forecast the outcome of the next meeting. There are numerous speaking engagements on the calendar, including Cleveland Fed President Hammack and Dallas Fed President Logan on Thursday, and New York Fed President Williams on Friday. Forecasters will be looking for clues to support the “hike every other meeting” thesis. executive_summary.text: 高按揭利率继续压制购房需求：10 月成屋销售、住宅签约量和按揭申请均下降，研究机构预计利率至 2027 年年中仍可能高于 7%，住房市场短期仍面临 affordability 压力。多户住宅表现分化：凤凰城吸纳强劲且空置率下降，AMH 保持高入住率和收入增长，但全国开发信心、CRE 信贷条件及公寓估值走弱，资本仍需关注融资与供给节奏。区域机会仍集中于具备就业和需求支撑的市场，DFW 获评 2027 年首选市场；同时门户市场许可量回升、部分 Sun Belt 市场许可量下降，供给扩张路径并不一致。
executive_summary.text_en: High mortgage rates continue to suppress homebuying: October existing-home sales, pending activity, and mortgage applications declined, while Zillow expects rates may remain above 7% through mid-2027. Multifamily performance is mixed: Phoenix absorption and AMH operations were strong, but developer confidence, CRE lending conditions, and apartment valuations weakened, keeping financing and supply timing in focus. Regional opportunities remain concentrated in markets with employment and demand support, with DFW ranked the top 2027 market; permitting is rising in gateway markets but falling in parts of the Sun Belt.
